text.p: Centocor Inc., a biotechnology company, announced Monday two encouraging studies using a new treatment for Crohn's disease, a chronic inflamation of the gastrointestinal tract.

The Malvern, Pennsylvania company said the studies tested a monoclonal antibody called cA2, or infliximab. "Data from both trials show that treatment with cA2 can have a beneficial effect on both the severity and number of symptoms associated with Crohn's disease," Centocor said in a statement released in Washington.

"The results are very encouraging," the statement quoted Richard P. MacDermott from the Crohn's & Colitis Foundation of America as saying. "It is possible that an important new therapy for Crohn's disease may be on the horizon."

The studies were conducted in 18 centers in North America and Europe over the last year and a half, Centocor said. In the first trial of 73 patients, there was an improvement after a single infusion of cA2 -- the level of disease activity dropped dramatically in 65 percent of patients. When four more infusions were given eight weeks apart, 60 percent of patients were able to achieve and maintain clinical remission.

The second study, of 94 patients, indicated that cA2 may be a valuable treatment for enterocutaneous fistulae, a painful, debilitating complication of the disease, the company said. Following a series of three cA2 infusions given two and four weeks apart, two-thirds of patients experienced closure of at least 50 percent of their fistulae, it said.
Centocor concentrates on research and development, manufacturing and market development of products and services that solve critical health care needs, the company said.
